title: Lesson 4: Close Read-aloud, Session 3: What Makes Day and Night
objective: Students will distinguish information learned from illustrations and text about the pattern of light and dark on earth and record observations about the sun and moon using adjectives in their writing.

what_is_taught.skill: distinguish information learned from illustrations and text
describe the pattern of light and dark on earth using details from text and illustrations
use adjectives to describe objects (sun, moon, stars)
fill in missing adjectives in a poem using an anchor chart
participate in group discussion using sentence stems and protocols
engage in partner talk to share ideas and reflections
conduct a hands-on experiment modeling earth's rotation and its effect on daylight and darkness
use scientific vocabulary related to earth's movement (e.g., rotate)
write observations using adjectives in complete sentences in a notebook
use classroom resources (word walls, charts) to support writing
demonstrate understanding of integrity and ethical behavior during group work

student_actions.recognition_identification: identify missing adjectives and scientific vocabulary in text and charts
student_actions.oral_production: participate in group and partner discussions, share ideas and reflections orally
student_actions.written_production: write sentences and draw pictures describing the sun and moon using adjectives in a notebook
student_actions.investigation_handson: engage in hands-on modeling of earth's rotation using flashlights and partner roles
student_actions.representation_modeling: model earth and sun positions during the experiment and represent ideas in writing and drawing
student_actions.reasoning_explanation: explain how earth's rotation causes day and night and justify use of adjectives
student_actions.comprehension_response: respond to questions about text and illustrations to describe patterns of light and dark on earth and poem content and meaning in writing and discussion

evidence.quote: Remind them that in previous lessons they listened to the poem being read aloud and listened for adjectives that describe the sun, moon, and stars.
Invite students to follow along as you read the poem aloud and track the print: 'The sun looks ______________.'
'Which adjective fits in the missing space?' (Responses will vary.)
As students share responses, use their ideas to fill in the missing adjective. (Example: 'The sun looks large and yellow.')
When all corrections have been made, read the corrected poem together with students.
'Can we add any more adjectives to describe the sun, moon, and stars to this chart?' (Responses will vary.)
'What is something at home or at school that we could describe using this adjective?' (Responses will vary)

Invite students to turn and talk to an elbow partner: 'What do we notice about how the illustrations and the text in the book help us to understand the pattern of light and dark on earth'? (The pictures and the words match, and they show part of earth in light and some in dark.)
Guide students through the close read-aloud of What Makes Day and Night using the Close Read-aloud Guide: What Makes Day and Night (Session 3; for teacher reference).
Before reading, provide white boards and dry-erase markers as an option for students to record (in drawing or writing) their ideas.

Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner: 'During the day, is the earth facing toward the sun, or away from the sun? How do you know?' (The earth is facing the sun during daytime. I know because the sun gives us light and warmth.)
Tell students that today they will work in groups to see how daylight turns into darkness as the earth rotates throughout the day.
Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner:
Using a total participation technique, invite responses from the group:
Display pages 22-23 of What Makes Day and Night. Say: 'Today you will work in pairs to re-create the illustrations on pages 22 and 23.'
Distribute fl ashlights. Tell students that one partner will model being the earth and the other partner will model being the sun by holding a flashlight.
Invite students to re-create the first illustration on page 22.
Tell students that they will now talk with a partner using the Pinky Partners protocol to discuss what they noticed about how the earth moves from daylight to darkness.
Guide students through the protocol.
Invite students to Think-Pair-Share with an elbow partner: 'How did you show integrity during the science activity?' (Responses will vary.)
Offer the following sentence stems as necessary:
Gather students back together and invite a few students to share out.
Remind students that they will keep working on using this habit of character throughout the unit when working with partners and small groups.

Remind them that earlier in the lesson they were introduced to the Adjectives anchor chart. Now they will look at a new set of sun and moon pictures and write about these pictures using adjectives from the anchor chart in their very own Sky notebook.
Invite students to turn and talk to an elbow partner:
Invite students to show a thumbs-up or touch their head if they are ready to begin writing and drawing about the sun and moon.
Transition students to their workspaces and invite them to begin working on page 1.
After 3 minutes of work time, recommend that students begin working on page 2.
Circulate and support students as necessary. Encourage them to use classroom resources (Word Walls, high-frequency word lists, and alphabet or letter sound combination charts).
Offer students specific, positive feedback on their use of adjectives. (Example: 'I noticed you were thinking about which adjectives best describe today's moon picture.')
For ELLs: Provide students with a sentence frame to support their writing in their Sky notebooks. (Example: The sun looks _____ and _____.')

teacher_actions.direct_instruction: Models reading the poem aloud, filling in missing adjectives, modeling the earth rotation experiment, and modeling classroom protocols for discussion and partner talk.
prompts_that_cue_student_response: What do you notice that's different about the poem today?
What words are missing in the empty spaces?
Which adjective fits in the missing space?
What do we notice about how the illustrations and the text in the book help us to understand the pattern of light and dark on earth?
During the day, is the earth facing toward the sun, or away from the sun? How do you know?
Have you experienced a time when you had to do the right thing even when it's hard? What was the scenario?
How did you show integrity during the science activity?

scope.breadth: The lesson covers understanding the pattern of day and night, earth's rotation, use of adjectives to describe celestial objects, and ethical behavior in group work.
scope.depth: Students engage in close reading, hands-on experiments, partner discussions, and independent writing to deepen understanding.

context.stimulus_provided: text, illustrations, photographs, poem, globe, flashlight

sections_covered.warm_up: Engaging the Learner: 'What We See: The Sun, Moon, and Stars' Poem
sections_covered.direct_instruction: Close Read-aloud, Session 3: What Makes Day and Night, Pages 16-20; Engaging the Scientist: Introducing Integrity and Modeling How the Earth Moves
sections_covered.differentiated_reinforce: Use of sentence stems and sentence frames for ELLs
sections_covered.differentiated_extend: Encouragement to add adjectives to the anchor chart and use classroom resources during writing

supports.english_language_learners: Provides sentence frames for writing, concrete examples and stories to explain abstract concepts like integrity, and visual labeling of photographs.
supports.universal_design_udl: Offers multiple means of engagement including partner talk, total participation techniques, use of whiteboards for drawing or writing, and use of visual aids like anchor charts and word walls.
supports.below_level_reinforce: Use of sentence stems and sentence frames, teacher modeling, and partner talk to scaffold understanding and expression.
supports.above_level_extend: Encourages students to add new adjectives to the anchor chart and to explain their reasoning during discussions.

assessment.method: Observation of student participation in discussions, poem completion, hands-on experiment, and independent writing in Sky notebooks.
assessment.recognition_vs_production: Both recognition (identifying adjectives and scientific concepts) and production (oral explanations, writing, and modeling) are assessed.

notes: The lesson integrates science content about earth's rotation with language arts skills including vocabulary development, comprehension of informational text, and writing using adjectives. It also incorporates social-emotional learning through the habit of character 'integrity.'
